products.name: Grammarly for Education
products.note: Institutional writing support; student data; FERPA compliance; generative AI features

reading.body:
Grammarly operates two distinct products, one general and one built specifically for institutional education use with FERPA compliance, both applying generative AI to text at the document level.

The company's market split reflects a familiar pattern in AI applications. General writing assistance reaches individual users across apps and websites. The education product isolates a regulated use case where data handling requirements are strict and institutional buyers have standardized procurement processes. Both products process documents broadly rather than targeting narrow tasks, which means they depend on language models large enough to handle varied writing contexts and quality levels.

This dual-product structure matters for compute intensity because institutional sales typically involve both higher volume and stricter data residency requirements. Educational institutions in different states may need models run on segregated infrastructure rather than shared cloud services. The education product's explicit reference to FERPA compliance signals that the company must manage student data differently from consumer data, which affects where and how its inference runs.

The data does not indicate whether Grammarly runs proprietary models or uses third-party inference. It notes the company's public claim about not monetizing user content for model training, but does not show how this constraint affects the models' size, cost, or performance. The 175 California law exposures reflect headquarters location rather than operational footprint. Revenue claims about employee savings are stated but not verified here.

profile_text.body:
Grammarly is a for-profit company founded in 2009 and headquartered in San Francisco, California. The company describes itself as offering AI writing assistance that works across apps and websites, providing personalized guidance, text generation, tone suggestions, and style-guide enforcement. It states that it does not sell or monetize user content, does not use it for advertising, and does not allow third-party service providers to train their models on user content.

The company's tracked products include Grammarly, a writing and editing tool that reads document text broadly, and Grammarly for Education, an institutional product aimed at student writing support with noted FERPA compliance and generative AI features. The company claims that organizations deploying Grammarly save an average of $5,000 per employee per year, and it references a productivity offering delivered through a product called Superhuman Go, described as combining writing support with productivity agents.

The held facts note 181 instances of California law exposure associated with Grammarly, which may reflect privacy policy disclosures, terms of service, or other regulatory acknowledgments directed at California residents. No litigation cases or MCP server registrations are currently recorded for the company.
